items.title: Employment Standards Act, 2000
items.says: The Employment Standards Act, 2000 sets employment standards that apply to an employee and employer when the employee's work is to be performed in Ontario, or in and outside Ontario where the outside work continues work done in Ontario, subject to listed exceptions.

source.expect: the employment standards set out in this Act apply

review.problem: Section 3 (1) only says when the Act's standards apply (work performed in Ontario); it does not list wages, hours, overtime, vacation, holidays, leaves or termination as the Act's contents.

items.title: O. Reg. 288/01 (Termination and Severance of Employment)
items.says: Section 2 (1) of this regulation lists employees who are not entitled to notice of termination or termination pay under Part XV of the Employment Standards Act, such as employees hired for a definite term or task and employees guilty of wilful misconduct that is not trivial and was not condoned.

source.expect: not entitled to notice of termination or termination pay

review.problem: Section 2 (1) lists employees not entitled to notice of termination or termination pay only; it says nothing about severance pay or mass-termination notice periods.

items.title: O. Reg. 285/01 (exemptions and special rules)
items.says: Section 8 of this regulation lists employees to whom the overtime pay Part of the Employment Standards Act does not apply, including a person whose work is supervisory or managerial in character and who may do other tasks only on an irregular or exceptional basis.

source.expect: supervisory or managerial in character

review.problem: Section 8 exempts listed employees from the overtime Part (Part VIII) only; hours-of-work exemptions are in section 4 and industry special rules are elsewhere in the regulation.

items.title: Human Rights Code
items.says: The Human Rights Code gives every person the right to equal treatment in employment without discrimination on listed grounds, and gives every employee the right to freedom from harassment in the workplace by the employer, the employer's agent or another employee on the grounds listed in subsection 5 (2).

source.expect: equal treatment with respect to employment without discrimination

review.problem: Subsection 5 (2) protects employees from workplace harassment on a list of grounds that does not include sex, so 'on those grounds' overstates it (sexual harassment is covered in s. 7).

items.title: Occupational Health and Safety Act
items.says: The Occupational Health and Safety Act defines workplace harassment as a course of vexatious comment or conduct against a worker in a workplace, including virtually, that is known or ought reasonably to be known to be unwelcome, and it includes workplace sexual harassment. The Act also defines workplace violence.

source.citation: Occupational Health and Safety Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. O.1
source.expect: engaging in a course of vexatious comment or conduct

review.problem: s. 1(1) is definitions only; employer duties and reprisal protection are in other sections.

items.title: Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997
items.says: A worker employed by a Schedule 1 employer, the worker's survivors and a Schedule 1 employer cannot start a lawsuit about the worker's injury or disease against any Schedule 1 employer or its directors, executive officers or workers; a Schedule 2 worker and survivors cannot sue the worker's own Schedule 2 employer or its directors, executive officers or workers. Exceptions apply, for example where another employer supplied a vehicle, machinery or equipment without workers to operate it.

source.citation: Workplace Safety and Insurance Act, 1997, S.O. 1997, c. 16, Sched. A
source.expect: not entitled to commence an action

review.problem: s. 28 does not describe benefits as no-fault, and the bar depends on Schedule 1 or Schedule 2 status, with conditions and exceptions in s. 28(3)-(4).

items.title: Limitations Act, 2002
items.says: The Limitations Act, 2002 sets the general time limit for starting a court case in Ontario, including a wrongful dismissal lawsuit.

source.expect: after the second anniversary of the day on which the

items.title: Courts of Justice Act
items.says: Under the Courts of Justice Act, the Small Claims Court hears actions for the payment of money where the amount claimed, not counting interest and costs, does not exceed the prescribed amount.

source.expect: jurisdiction in any action for the payment of money

review.problem: Section 23 (1) only sets the Small Claims Court's monetary jurisdiction; it does not establish the courts generally or govern interest, costs or appeals.

items.title: Canada Labour Code (federally regulated work)
items.says: Under the Canada Labour Code, a person who has been dismissed and considers the dismissal unjust may make a written complaint to the Head, if they completed 12 consecutive months of continuous employment with the employer and are not a member of a group of employees subject to a collective agreement.

source.citation: Canada Labour Code, R.S.C. 1985, c. L-2
source.expect: may make a complaint in writing to the Head

review.problem: s. 240(1) gives no examples of federal industries and does not mention the Ontario Employment Standards Act; it sets conditions (12 consecutive months, not under a collective agreement).

items.title: Employment Insurance Act
items.says: A claimant, another person who is the subject of a Commission decision, or the claimant's employer may ask the Commission to reconsider the decision within 30 days after it is communicated to them, or any further time the Commission allows; the Commission must reconsider it.

source.expect: for a reconsideration of that decision

review.problem: s. 112(1) covers reconsideration only; it does not describe benefits generally, and under s. 113 an appeal of a reconsideration decision now goes to the Employment Insurance Board of Appeal, not the Social Security Tribunal.

items.title: Who the Employment Standards Act covers
items.says: The Act applies when the employee's work is done in Ontario, or is done in and outside Ontario where the outside work continues the work done in Ontario.

source.expect: the employee's work is to be performed in Ontario

items.title: Federal jobs are not covered
items.says: The Ontario Act does not apply where the employment relationship falls under the law-making power of Parliament (federally regulated work).

source.expect: within the legislative jurisdiction of the Parliament of Canada

items.title: People the Act does not apply to
items.says: The Act does not apply to some people at all, such as secondary school students in a school work experience program, people working in an approved college or university program, and some other listed individuals.

source.expect: This Act does not apply with respect to the following

items.title: Who is an "employee"
items.says: An employee includes a person who performs work for an employer for wages, a person who supplies services to an employer for wages, some trainees, and homeworkers. It also includes a person who used to be an employee.

source.expect: performs work for an employer for wages

items.title: Related businesses treated as one employer
items.says: Where associated or related activities or businesses are or were carried on by or through an employer and one or more other persons, they are all treated as one employer under the Act, and they are jointly and severally liable for wages owing to an employee of any of them (with exceptions for some shareholders and the Crown).

source.expect: shall all be treated as one employer for the purposes

review.problem: The Act says related employers 'shall all be treated as one employer', not that they 'can' be; the item turns a mandatory rule into a discretionary one.

items.title: Treating an employee as a contractor is not allowed
items.says: An employer must not treat a person who is an employee as if they were not an employee under the Act, for example by calling them an independent contractor.

source.expect: as if the person were not an employee under this

items.title: No contracting out of minimum standards
items.says: Employers and employees cannot agree to give up an employment standard. Any agreement to contract out of or waive a standard is void.

source.expect: any such contracting out or waiver is void

items.title: A better contract term wins
items.says: If a contract term or another law gives the employee a greater benefit on the same subject than the Act does, the better term applies instead of the standard.

source.expect: provide a greater benefit to an employee than the employment

items.title: The Act does not take away court remedies
items.says: Subject to the rules about choosing between an ESA claim and a lawsuit, the Act does not affect an employee's civil remedies against the employer.

source.expect: no civil remedy of an employee against his or her

items.title: Notice to the Director of a civil case under the Act
items.says: An employee who starts a civil case against the employer under the Act serves notice of the case on the Director of Employment Standards, on the approved form, on or before the date the case is set down for trial.

source.expect: notice of the proceeding shall be served on the Director

items.title: Managers and supervisors and overtime
items.says: Overtime pay rules do not apply to a person whose work is supervisory or managerial in character, even if they sometimes do other tasks on an irregular or exceptional basis. Other jobs have their own exemptions in the regulation.

source.expect: who may perform non-supervisory or non-managerial tasks on an irregular

items.title: Unionized employees use the grievance process
items.says: If the employer is bound by a collective agreement, the Act is enforceable as if it were part of that agreement, and an employee represented by the union may not file an ESA complaint about those matters unless the Director permits it.

source.expect: may not file a complaint alleging a contravention of this

review.problem: Section 99 does not mention a grievance process and the item drops subsection (6), under which the Director may still permit a represented employee to file a complaint.

items.title: What counts as "wages"
items.says: Wages include money owed under the employment contract and any payment the Act requires. They do not include tips, discretionary gifts or bonuses not tied to hours, production or efficiency, or expenses and travel allowances.

source.expect: monetary remuneration payable by an employer to an employee

items.title: Regular pay period and pay day
items.says: An employer must set a recurring pay period and pay day, and pay all wages earned in each pay period (other than accruing vacation pay) by that pay day.

source.expect: shall establish a recurring pay period and a recurring pay

items.title: Final pay when a job ends
items.says: When employment ends, the employer must pay the wages owed by the later of seven days after the job ends and the employee's next regular pay day.

source.expect: seven days after the employment ends

items.title: Pay statement on every pay day
items.says: On or before each pay day, the employer must give a written statement showing the pay period, wage rate, gross wages and how they were calculated, each deduction and its purpose, and the net amount paid.

source.expect: the employer shall give to the employee a written statement

items.title: Statement with final pay
items.says: When final pay is due, the employer must give a written statement showing any termination pay, severance pay and vacation pay, how they were calculated, and the other usual pay statement information.

source.expect: the gross amount of any termination pay or severance pay

items.title: No deductions without authority
items.says: An employer cannot hold back wages, make deductions, or make the employee pay wages back, unless a statute or court order allows it or the employee gave written authorization (and even then, not for some things the Act lists).

source.expect: An employer shall not withhold wages payable to an employee

items.title: Employer must keep employment records
items.says: An employer must record information about each employee, including the dates and times worked and the hours worked each day and week; for an employee paid a salary, the employer may instead record only certain excess hours, or nothing about hours if the hours and overtime rules do not apply.

source.expect: The number of hours the employee worked in each day

review.problem: Section 15 sets out what must be recorded but says nothing about the records mattering in disputes, and it lets an employer of a salaried employee skip the daily and weekly hours record in some cases.

items.title: Minimum wage
items.says: An employer must pay employees at least the minimum wage. Compliance is checked pay period by pay period.

source.expect: An employer shall pay employees at least the minimum wage

items.title: Three-hour rule when sent home early
items.says: If an employee who regularly works more than three hours a day is required to come in but works less than three hours, though available to work longer, the employer must pay wages for three hours, with exceptions for fire, power failure, storms and similar causes.

source.expect: the employer shall pay the employee wages for three hours

items.title: Limits on hours of work
items.says: An employer cannot require or permit an employee to work more than eight hours a day (or the employee's longer regular day) or 48 hours a week, unless the employee has made a written agreement allowing more.

source.expect: no employer shall require or permit an employee to work

items.title: Daily and weekly rest periods
items.says: An employer must give at least 11 hours in a row off work each day, generally eight hours between shifts, and either 24 hours in a row off each week or 48 hours in a row in each two-week period.

source.expect: at least 11 consecutive hours free from performing work

items.title: Eating periods
items.says: An employer must give a 30-minute eating period so that the employee does not work more than five hours in a row without one. It can be split into two periods if both agree.

source.expect: eating period of at least 30 minutes

items.title: Overtime pay after 44 hours
items.says: An employer must pay overtime of at least one and one-half times the employee's regular rate for each hour worked over 44 in a work week, unless the job is exempt or a valid averaging arrangement applies.

source.expect: one and one-half times his or her regular rate

items.title: Equal pay for equal work (sex)
items.says: An employer cannot pay an employee of one sex less than an employee of the other sex for substantially the same kind of work in the same establishment, requiring substantially the same skill, effort and responsibility, under similar working conditions.

source.expect: they perform substantially the same kind of work in the

items.title: How tips must be paid
items.says: Tips and other gratuities owed to an employee must be paid by cash, cheque payable only to the employee, direct deposit or another prescribed method.

source.expect: An employer shall pay an employee's tips or other gratuities

items.title: Employer cannot keep employees' tips
items.says: An employer cannot withhold, deduct from, or make an employee hand over tips, except as the Act allows. Tips taken wrongly are a debt owed to the employee and can be enforced like unpaid wages.

source.expect: An employer shall not withhold tips or other gratuities from

items.title: Tip pools
items.says: An employer may collect tips and redistribute them among some or all employees, but the employer and its directors or shareholders cannot share in the pool, except a sole proprietor, partner, director or shareholder who regularly does to a substantial degree the same work as the employees sharing in it (or as tipped employees of other employers in the same industry).

review.problem: The item says only a sole proprietor or partner may share in the pool, but subsection 14.4 (5) gives directors and shareholders the same exception when they regularly do the same work to a substantial degree.

items.title: Ontario's public holidays
items.says: The public holidays are New Year's Day, Family Day, Good Friday, Victoria Day, Canada Day, Labour Day, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day, December 26, and any day prescribed by regulation.

source.expect: Family Day, being the third Monday in February

items.title: Day off with public holiday pay
items.says: If a public holiday falls on a day that would normally be a working day, and the employee is not on vacation, the employer must give the day off and pay public holiday pay.

source.expect: the employer shall give the employee the day off work

items.title: Last and first scheduled day rule
items.says: An employee loses the public holiday entitlement if, without reasonable cause, they do not work all of their last regularly scheduled day before the holiday or their first regularly scheduled day after it.

source.expect: fails, without reasonable cause, to work all of his or

items.says: Public holiday pay equals the regular wages earned and vacation pay payable in the four work weeks before the week of the holiday, divided by 20. Premium pay is at least one and one-half times the regular rate.

source.expect: in the four work weeks before the work week in

items.title: Working on a public holiday
items.says: An employee and employer may agree that the employee will work a public holiday that would ordinarily be a working day. The employer then pays regular wages for the hours worked and gives a substitute day off with public holiday pay, or, if both agree, pays public holiday pay plus premium pay for each hour worked.

items.title: Holiday on a day off or during vacation
items.says: If a public holiday falls on a day the employee would not normally work, or while on vacation, the employer must give a substitute day off with public holiday pay, generally within three months (or up to 12 months if both agree).

items.title: Vacation time

items.says: Vacation pay is generally paid as a lump sum before the vacation starts. Other timing is allowed in some cases, such as paying it on each pay if the employee agrees and it is shown separately on the pay statement.

items.title: Child death leave

items.title: Domestic or sexual violence leave

items.title: Reservist leave

items.title: Job search leave during a notice period

items.title: Presumption of reasonable notice
items.says: An employment contract for an indefinite term carries an implied term that the employer gives reasonable notice to end it without cause, unless the contract clearly and lawfully says otherwise. items.title: How long reasonable notice is (Bardal factors)
items.says: Courts set reasonable notice case by case, considering factors including, but not limited to, the character of the employment, length of service, the employee's age and the availability of similar employment given the employee's experience, training and qualifications.

items.says: An employer can dismiss without notice only for just cause: misconduct so serious that it is incompatible with the employment relationship, judged in context and with proportionality. The employer has to prove it.

items.title: Constructive dismissal

items.title: Damages for bad faith in the manner of dismissal
items.says: If the employee proves that the manner of dismissal caused mental distress that was in the contemplation of the parties, damages are awarded to reflect the actual harm, not through an extension of the notice period.
